title: Bundle design: licensing, configuration model, footprint, sign-in
description: Settle the questions that decide whether and how CourtHive can be bundled, before any build work. (1) Licensing and permission: confirm each component's licence (competition-factory-server and TMX declare MIT; courthive-public declares none) and get CourtHive's author's agreement in writing to redistributing built images from forks; record the attribution required. Jim makes that contact. (2) Configuration: TMX bakes its server address in at compile time (src/platform/web.ts) and builds from upstream's blank production settings white-screen or fail to log in; determine the smallest change that yields one club-neutral build - same-origin defaults, the base path, and the socket settings already needed behind Caddy (origin-only path, polling transport). (3) Footprint: measure memory and disk for app + Postgres + Redis + tournament server on the smallest sensible server and state a minimum specification. (4) Sign-in: decided on 2026-11-21 - jim-dot-tennis is the identity source and CourtHive trusts tokens it mints (WI-152); design the mechanism (signing key, token lifetime, role mapping, how CourtHive's own login is switched off). (5) Upgrades: how the forks track upstream and how a club receives a CourtHive update, given the calendar backfill step that had to be run by hand between two server migrations. Deliver a short design note in docs/ and update the downstream work items if the findings change them.

recommended_model.name: Fable 5.2
recommended_model.rationale: Open-ended design across three unfamiliar codebases with legal and operational constraints; the decisions here shape the whole sprint.

acceptance_criteria: Written permission (or a clear refusal) from CourtHive's author is on file, and every component has an explicit licence that allows redistribution
A chosen configuration approach with a proof: one build of TMX and of the public pages served correctly under two different hostnames
A measured minimum server specification, with and without the tournament stack
A designed single sign-on mechanism with jim-dot-tennis as the identity source (feeds WI-152)
An upgrade policy: which upstream versions are bundled, how often, and how data migrations run unattended
docs/courthive_bundle_design.md written; WI-143 to WI-147 amended where needed

notes: If permission is refused or a component cannot be licensed, the fallback is documenting how a club points jim-dot-tennis at its own separately installed CourtHive - raise this with Jim immediately rather than proceeding.
Sibling repositories live beside this one: ../competition-factory-server, ../TMX, ../courthive-public (and ../courthive-components, ../factory).
Known hazards from past deploys: pnpm link overrides must be removed when rebasing the forks; socket.io behind Caddy needs the origin-only path and polling transport.

context.user_story: As the maintainer, I want to know the bundle is permitted and practical before investing in it.
context.programme: Club-readiness programme (sprints 019-024). Agreed constraints: BHPLTA clubs only; each club self-hosts its own instance; the original author must have no access to any other club's instance (no seeded accounts, no shared or default secrets, no phone-home); passkeys are the default sign-in with passwords as an optional fallback; the captain role is real; SQLite is the only supported database; CourtHive is bundled as an opt-in part of the package so clubs can run their own club championships.

status_note: Design rewritten the same day after the owner chose latest upstream and asked for tournament-only accounts. Every component is MIT with a licence file at the bundled revisions, so no permission is outstanding; a courtesy note to CourtHive's author remains the owner's to send. Config, footprint, sign-in and upgrade findings are proven in the design note.
